newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam inflation rate ends 1996 at six-month high.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam inflation rate ends 1996 at six-month high.

text.p: Vietnam's consumer price index rose 1.0 percent in December from the previous month, lifting the annual inflation rate to a six-month high of 4.5 percent, the General Statistics Office said on Thursday.

December's month-on-month rise was the biggest since February and could ease concerns, triggered by a four-month run of falling prices mid-year, that the economy may now be coming off the boil, analysts said.

A tight monetary policy, largely through bank-by-bank credit ceilings, and an austere fiscal stance have helped drive the annual inflation rate down to end this year at 4.5 percent compared with 12.7 percent at the end of 1995.

However, December's price rise appeared to have been generated by a government decision to raise prices for oil products, including petrol, by between five and 12 percent due to pressure from global cost increases.
The statistics office's data showed fuel prices up 22.8 percent from a year ago and up 6.7 percent from November.
A weighty component of the index, rice and other staples, was up 3.0 percent on the month but only 0.2 percent higher than the end of 1995.

A bumper rice crop and an improvement in distribution kept a lid on rice prices throughout most of the year, but analysts said heavy flooding in several parts of the country probably contributed to the year-end spike.

The government, anxious not to see a repeat of the hyperinflation that plagued the economy before market-style reforms began to bite in the early 1990s, has made the pursuit of low inflation a policy priority.
Analysts say that while the authorities appear to have tamed inflation, they are now faced with the more fundamental problem of rapidly widening current account and trade gaps.
The government has forecast a 1996 trade deficit of around $4.0 billion for this year, equivalent to around 18 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), compared with $2.3 billion in 1995.

"Despite the government's prudent macroeconomic policies...the trade and current account deficits have widened considerably in 1996," the World Bank said in a recent report. "Current account deficits in this range are not sustainable in the medium term."

The World Bank noted that there had been a significant real appreciation of the local currency, the dong, against the currencies of its main trading partners since mid-1995, but fell short of recommending a devaluation.
Earlier this year the central State Bank of Vietnam considered devaluation as a means of making imports more expensive and exports cheaper, but opted for a policy of very gradual depreciation.
The dong was quoted at 11,144/55 per dollar in Vietnam's tiny interbank market on Thursday, down about 0.6 percent from its level of 11,085 a month ago.
